FACT SHEET: POLLARD STREET TOOL LIBRARY

About us
- A tool library in Ferrisham. Members borrow tools and household equipment for a week at a time instead of buying them.
- A community interest company set up in 2024 by Ines Marlow and Arjun Tate. Neither of us is paid. Ines presents; Arjun will be there for questions.
- Premises: a former launderette at 14 Pollard Street. Rent is £650 a month, covered until March 2028 by a Ferrisham Town Council grant.
- The line on our website (we wrote it in 2024 and we're not attached to it): 'We believe everyone deserves access to the tools they need to build a better, more sustainable community.'

The funder
- Calder-Wynn Foundation, Neighbourhood Resilience Fund: grants of up to £40,000 over up to two years.
- Their guidance says panels 'will want to know how the work continues after the grant ends'.
- Decision on 4 December 2026. Funded projects can start on 1 February 2027.

Year one: 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 (all of this is in the report the panel has read)
- Our target was 500 members by 31 March 2026. We had 287.
- Why we think we fell short: we opened 10 weeks late because the lease was delayed; we're only open for two sessions a week (Wednesday 5–8pm and Saturday 10am–2pm), all run by volunteers; and people without a car told us they couldn't get bulky things like carpet cleaners home.
- 1,146 loans in the year.
- Most borrowed: cordless drill, carpet cleaner, ladder, pressure washer.
- 612 items in stock, 94% of them donated.
- Membership is £15 a year, or pay what you can for anyone on benefits. 41% of members joined on pay what you can.
- 23 active volunteers.
- Since the report: 341 members on 31 August 2026.

The ask
- £36,400 over 24 months (1 February 2027 to 31 January 2029):
  - £22,800 for a part-time coordinator, two days a week for 24 months
  - £6,900 for a second-hand electric cargo trike with a lockable box, for deliveries within 2 miles
  - £6,700 for volunteer training, first-aid certificates and extra insurance for the new opening days
- What changes: we add Tuesdays and Fridays, 10am–4pm, run by the coordinator with volunteers. Deliveries by trike on those two days.

After the grant
- From February 2028 we'd charge £3 per delivery. From April 2028 standard membership would go up from £15 to £20 a year (pay what you can stays).
- The aim is for fees to cover the coordinator from February 2029. We haven't tested whether members will accept either change.

What we don't have
- No member quotes or stories we have permission to use.
- No survey data.

material:
WINCH HOUSE SAUNA: NOTES FROM MAREN

What it is
- A wood-fired sauna in the old lifeboat winch house on the east slipway at Orwick harbour, just behind the lifeboat station.
- Seats 8. Dev and I built the benches from larch.
- Your cold dip is the sea, straight off the slipway. There's a cold outdoor shower too.
- There is no lifeguard. Swimming is at your own risk (we have to say this).
- Changing is a small shed with two cubicles. No lockers, so bring as little as you can.
- Access: step-free to the changing shed, but there are three steep steps down into the sauna itself.
- Open every day except Tuesday. The first session is at 7am; the last one starts at 8pm.
- Sessions go ahead in any weather. If the harbour master closes the slipway for a storm, we cancel and refund you in full.
- Run by me (Maren Holt) and Dev Aluko. We opened in May 2025.
- The winter sunrise sessions are the ones people talk about: the sun comes up over the breakwater during the 7am session.

Prices (exactly as written)
- Shared session, 75 minutes: £15
- Off-peak shared session (weekdays, starting before 2pm): £11
- 10-session card: £120, valid for 12 months from purchase, for shared sessions at any time
- Private hire of the whole sauna, up to 8 people, 90 minutes: £110
- Towel hire: £3

Booking terms
- Booking is online only. We can't take walk-ins.
- Cancel or move your booking up to 24 hours before and you get a full refund. After that we can't refund, but you can give your place to a friend.
- Under-16s can't come to shared sessions. They're welcome at private hires with an adult.

What to bring
- Swimwear (you must wear it), a towel (or hire one), a water bottle, and something for your feet on the slipway.

Getting here
- Park in the Orwick harbour car park (pay and display), 3 minutes' walk.

Buttons
- Both buttons go to the booking page. Our email and phone number are in the site footer, so the homepage doesn't need them.

NOTES: PENNOCK'S IDENTITY, DIRECTION 'COUNTER' (Studio Wend)

The client
- Pennock's Hardware: a family hardware business with three branches (Market Street in Aldermere, which is the original shop, plus Tollgate Road and Brookside retail park) and two delivery vans.
- Founded in 1964 by Alma Pennock at 2 Market Street. Ruth is her granddaughter.

What they told us at kick-off (their words)
- Ruth: 'We want to look like we've been here sixty years, not like we're stuck there.'
- Ruth: younger homeowners think Pennock's is 'the old man's shop'. She wants them to feel it's for them.
- Sol: 'Don't lose the trade.' The plumbers and builders who come in at 7am are about half the turnover.
- Both: everything ready for the relaunch on Monday 1 March 2027.

The direction: 'Counter'
- Wordmark redrawn from the hand-painted sign over the original shop at 2 Market Street.
- Two main colours: 'door green', matched to the original shop door, and 'tag yellow', from the old paper price tags.
- The price-tag shape runs through everything: offers, aisle signs, the website and the vans.
- Vans: green, with the wordmark large on both sides and the phone number on the back doors. We printed a full-size van panel and read it across our yard: clear at 40 metres.
- The trade counter gets its own sign in the same lettering: 'Trade — open from 7am'. Trade customers get green tags on their account cards.
- Not tested with customers yet.

The known risk
- Market Street is in a conservation area, so the new fascia colour needs consent from Aldermere District Council. That can take up to 8 weeks.
- Once there's consent, the sign-maker needs 10 weeks to make and fit the fascia.
- If we submit on Monday 19 October and the council takes the full 8 weeks, the new fascia goes up around 22 February, about a week before the relaunch. If the council asks for changes, Market Street probably won't have its new sign on 1 March.
- Tollgate Road, Brookside and the vans don't need consent and aren't affected.
- At a pre-application meeting on 2 October, the conservation officer said she had no objection in principle to the green but wants to see a sample board on the building before she decides.

The decision
- We need Ruth and Sol to approve 'Counter' as the final direction by Friday 16 October, so we can submit the council application on Monday 19 October and brief the sign-maker on the vans.
- If they approve later than that, Market Street almost certainly misses 1 March.

material:
PROJECT NOTES: KESSFORD COMMUNITY ARCHIVE ONLINE COLLECTION
Tern & Tally (Jo Tallis and Sam Okafor)

The client
- Kessford Community Archive: a volunteer-run local history archive in a back room of Kessford Library. 14 regular volunteers, most of them retired.
- About 3,400 photographs of the town from the 1890s to the 1990s, catalogued on handwritten index cards. The only way to search was to come in on a Tuesday or Thursday and ask.

The brief
- Get the photographs online and searchable.
- An online form for booking the reading room.

Constraints
- Budget: £9,000.
- About 10 weeks: 23 March to 3 June 2026.
- It had to run on the library's existing website system. We couldn't install anything new.
- The volunteers would do all the data entry, and many of them weren't confident with computers.
- The captions on the cards were inconsistent, and a lot of the photos had no date or only a guess.

What we did
- Designed a catalogue entry form with six fields. We watched three volunteers use the first version: they typed everything in capitals, because the old cards were in capitals. We changed the form to accept capitals and tidy them up.
- Ran two training sessions in the archive room and wrote a one-page guide that sits next to the computer.
- Built search by street. We compiled a list of 212 street names, including 31 that have since been renamed, so a search for Chapel Row also finds photos filed under its old name, Tanner's Lane.
- Designed a printed leaflet for the reading room explaining how to search.

What happened
- Launched on 3 June 2026 with 1,900 of the 3,400 photographs catalogued and online. The volunteers are adding the rest at their own pace; there's no end date.
- We'd planned a filter by decade. We dropped it before launch because too many photos had no reliable date.
- The reading room booking form was cut: the library's system couldn't support it. Bookings are still by phone.
- We have no numbers on use.

Approved quote
- Nadia Pell, volunteer coordinator, Kessford Community Archive: 'It's the first system we've had that the volunteers don't need me standing over them to use. That's not nothing.'

What we'd like readers to take away
- That we're good at working with volunteers and within tight constraints.

AGENCY DRAFT

About Us

At Pinder & Osei, we are passionate about delivering innovative, end-to-end catering equipment solutions that empower hospitality businesses to achieve operational excellence. Founded in 2009, we have grown into an award-winning team of dedicated professionals with over 50 years of combined industry experience.

We understand that in today's fast-paced foodservice landscape, downtime is simply not an option. That's why we offer a comprehensive 24/7 nationwide service, leveraging cutting-edge diagnostic technology to deliver industry-leading response times and first-time fix rates.

Our holistic approach means we partner with you every step of the way, from preventative maintenance to emergency repairs, ensuring your kitchen operates at peak performance. Whether you're a bustling restaurant, a busy school kitchen or a care facility, our bespoke service plans are tailored to your unique needs. No job is too big or too small.

At the heart of everything we do are our core values: integrity, reliability and customer-centricity. We believe in building long-lasting relationships founded on trust and transparency, and we pride ourselves on going above and beyond to exceed our clients' expectations every single time.

Our highly skilled engineers are fully certified across a wide range of equipment, including combination ovens, fryers, warewashers, refrigeration and extraction systems. We are committed to continuous improvement and invest heavily in ongoing training to stay ahead of the curve in a rapidly evolving industry.

Discover the Pinder & Osei difference today. Get in touch with our friendly, knowledgeable team to find out how we can help your business thrive.

THE FACTS (all checked)
- Pinder & Osei Catering Engineers, based in Wennick.
- Started in 2011 by Gwen Pinder and Kofi Osei. Before that, Gwen spent 8 years and Kofi 11 years as engineers for a national catering equipment company.
- There are five of us: Gwen and Kofi, two more engineers (Aled Price and Priya Nair), and Marcy Dunne, who runs the office and answers the phone.
- We repair and service commercial kitchen equipment: combination ovens, ovens and ranges, fryers, dishwashers and glasswashers, fridges, freezers and cold rooms, and extraction. We don't do domestic appliances.
- All four engineers are qualified to work on commercial gas appliances.
- We cover kitchens within 40 miles of Wennick.
- About 60 kitchens have a service contract with us: restaurants, pubs, two school kitchens and a care home. For contract customers we aim to be on site within 4 hours, 7am–10pm, seven days a week.
- Everyone else: we usually get to you the next working day.
- Each van carries about 400 of the parts we use most, so a lot of repairs are finished on the first visit. We don't keep figures on this.
- We don't sell new equipment. When something isn't worth repairing, we tell you, and we've no reason to push a replacement.
- Marcy answers the phone 8am–6pm on weekdays. Contract customers have a separate out-of-hours number.
- Our phone number is in the site header, so the page doesn't need it.

request: I'm applying to the Estuary Screen Fund's short film scheme and they want a treatment: 350–500 words, present tense, third person, telling the whole story including the ending. material:
LOW WATER (working title)
A 12-minute short. Small budget.

Fixed points
- Skerrow: a small tidal island reached by a causeway that floods twice a day.
- There's one café on the island. Nell Achterberg, 61, has run it alone since her husband, Piet, died two winters ago.
- Her daughter, Ros, 29, a junior doctor in the city, turns up without warning on the afternoon low tide. She hasn't been back since the funeral.
- The object: the tide clock above the café counter. Piet set it 20 minutes fast so that visitors would always leave in good time. Nell has never corrected it.
- Ros is due on shift at 7am tomorrow. If she misses this evening's crossing, she'll miss her shift.
- The ending has to turn on the clock.

Budget rules
- One location, the café, plus the causeway.
- No more than three speaking parts.
- No flashbacks.
- No one is ever in physical danger. I don't want a rescue.

Nice to have, not essential
- Some of it happens while there are still customers in the café.
- Nell and Ros are both a bit funny.

Tells the ending: it's clear what happens, including whether Ros leaves on the evening crossing; no cliffhanger, open question or teaser.

Keeps every fixed point unchanged: Skerrow and its causeway; Nell Achterberg, 61, running the café alone; Piet, died two winters ago; Ros, 29, junior doctor, arriving unannounced on the afternoon low tide, first time back since the funeral; the tide clock set 20 minutes fast by Piet and never corrected by Nell; Ros's 7am shift.
The ending turns on the tide clock: the fact that it's 20 minutes fast, or someone changing it, directly shapes the outcome.

TALK NOTES: 'Where's X-ray?'
Northern Wayfinding Forum, Hall B, 2pm, 25 minutes.

Me (the chair covers this): Tamsin Rook, head of wayfinding at Orla Valley Hospital. Twelve years there; before that I was a stage manager in theatre.

The clipboard week
- March 2025. I stood by the main reception desk at Orla Valley for five days, 8am to 6pm, and wrote down every question people asked the two receptionists.
- 1,312 questions in five days.
- 390 of them were some version of 'Where's X-ray?'
- The sign over the main corridor said 'Imaging and Radiology'. It had said that since the building opened in 2009. There wasn't a single sign anywhere that said 'X-ray'.
- On the Friday evening I counted the signs in the main corridor: 214.
- A man in a dressing gown asked me, not the receptionists: 'Is Imaging the same as X-ray, or is that somewhere else?' I didn't know whether it was my place to answer him.
- The Monday after, we changed that one sign. What happened next comes later in the talk.

The point of the talk (for the end, not the opening): signs should use the words people say out loud, not the names on the organisation chart.

How I talk: plain and fairly dry. Not jokey. I don't do rhetorical questions.

DRAFT

The Piano

When Mum moved into Elm Court last spring, the hardest thing to deal with was her piano. It was an upright my grandad bought second-hand in 1961, and it had been in the front room at Lark Road my whole life. Mum played it every Sunday, mostly hymns. She always said the D above middle C stuck because of 'the damp of '87', and none of us ever got round to fixing it.

Honestly, it was an incredibly difficult time. I was feeling so many emotions at once: sadness, guilt, frustration. I rang three dealers and none of them were interested. One of them said they're all firewood now, which I found quite upsetting. I suppose I felt like nobody understood what it meant to us.

In the end I put it on the local selling page, free to a good home, buyer collects, and a man rang that evening. He came on the Saturday with his daughter, who looked about fourteen, in a van he'd borrowed from work. She sat down with her coat still on and played a scale, and of course the D stuck. I told her about the damp of '87 and she laughed. It was a really emotional moment and I had to go into the kitchen for a minute.

Getting it out was a whole saga. Her dad had to take the front door off its hinges, and it took the three of us nearly an hour to get it down the steps. Before they left he gave me two twenty-pound notes, folded up small, even though the advert said free. I tried to give them back but he wouldn't have it. It was a lovely gesture. I stood on the pavement for a long time afterwards, feeling completely drained but also strangely at peace.

I kept the stool. Her music was still inside it: the Sunday hymn book, and a book of film themes I never once heard her play.

The next time I visited Mum, I was nervous about telling her, but I needn't have been. All she said was, 'Did the D stick?' I said yes, and she laughed properly for the first time in months. It made me realise how much the piano had meant to all of us.

Looking back, I've learned that letting go of things can be a gift, and that music doesn't live in objects but in the people who play it. Sometimes the hardest goodbyes turn out to be the most beautiful beginnings.
